name: Easy Peasy All-in-One Homeschool
line: Easy Peasy follows a fixed order of daily lessons. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Easy Peasy: Easy Peasy follows a fixed order of daily lessons. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Easy Peasy places a learner with a test at the start, then follows a fixed order of daily lessons [1][5]. From grade 5 on the lessons are built on outside videos and exercises [7][8]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. Every answer, right or wrong, updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Easy Peasy places a learner with a placement test, which it says is not meant as an ongoing assessment [5][9]. After that a learner follows a fixed order of daily lessons, and the parent moves a child to the next or previous course with buttons [1][3].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Easy Peasy the unit is the day's lesson, a numbered list of steps. In EP Math 1 that is often a video or a song, an online practice activity, then a written or hands-on task [6]. From Math 5/6 on, the steps send learners to outside videos, mostly from Khan Academy, and to exercises on other sites [7][8].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After each problem AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. In EP Math 1 the parent checks the work [6]. Worksheet answers sit on password-protected pages [3][8]. In Math 5/6 the exercises are on outside sites, and any checking is done by the site that hosts them [7]. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, in many ages and subjects, feedback that explains had the largest effect [13].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. An answer after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Math 5/6 asks a learner to stay on an exercise until they get five in a row right, on the outside site that hosts it [7]. Easy Peasy's own planner is, in its FAQ's words, "essentially a digital bookmark" [3][10]. Going back a course is a step the parent takes [3].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Easy Peasy's math courses include occasional review lessons [6][7]. We found no schedule that brings a learned skill back in those pages or the FAQ [3][6][7]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [14].

reasons.title: The adult's part
reasons.body: In AMP the adult does not plan, teach or grade. Parents and teachers see a level for each part of math and the actual problems behind every number, and each lesson has a guide for the adult. In Easy Peasy the parent supplies a computer and internet, stays available and keeps the records [2]. The FAQ makes the parent responsible for creating, maintaining and providing them [3].

rows.range: Preschool through grade 8. Math runs from Kinder Math and More to Pre-Algebra; Algebra 1 is on its high school site [4][5].
rows.start: A placement test for kindergarten to grade 8, plus a math placement guide. Not meant as an ongoing assessment [5][9].
rows.teaching: In EP Math 1, daily lessons of linked videos, songs, online practice and hands-on tasks [6]. From Math 5/6, mostly outside videos and exercises, including Khan Academy [7][8].
rows.next: A fixed order of daily lessons [1]. The parent moves a child with next-course or previous-course buttons [3].
rows.mastery: Math 5/6: five in a row correct on an outside exercise before moving on [7]. Easy Peasy's planner is a bookmark [3].
rows.review: Occasional review lessons [6][7]. No schedule that brings learned skills back found in the pages we read [3][6][7].
rows.print: Printable worksheets and workbooks; some math levels come as offline books [3][8]. One set of pages per course.
rows.adult: Supplies a computer, stays available and keeps records [2]. In Math 1, checks the work and helps with hands-on tasks [6].
rows.reports: The parent creates, maintains and provides records [3]. The My EP planner marks days complete [10].
rows.evidence: None found in the pages we read, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [11][12].

theirs: Easy Peasy All-in-One Homeschool is an online Christian curriculum for preschool through grade 8. Lee Giles began it in 2011 by putting her own children's assignments online [1][2]. It covers reading, math, science, Spanish, Bible, art, music, PE and health, and logic, with 180 days of lessons in each grade [1]. High school courses, Algebra 1 among them, are on a sister site [1][4].

Each day's lesson is a numbered list of steps. In EP Math 1 that is often a video or a song, an online practice activity, then a written or hands-on task [6]. From Math 5/6 on, the lessons link mostly to Khan Academy videos and to exercises on other sites, and it suggests about 30 minutes a day [7][8]. In EP Math 1 the parent checks the work [6]. Throughout, the parent keeps the records and moves a child between courses [2][3].
credit: Early math is hands-on: videos, songs, and tasks with real objects such as coins, with links to fact practice [6].
Math 5/6 asks for five in a row right on an exercise before a learner moves on [7].
Math sits inside one daily plan for every subject [1].

theirs: We found no outcome study of Easy Peasy All-in-One Homeschool on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [1][3][11][12].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, in many ages and subjects, feedback that explains had the largest average effect (0.49), the correct answer alone 0.32 and right or wrong alone 0.05 [13]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [14]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want math as one part of a daily plan for every subject, with hands-on work in the early grades.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want every answer checked at once and followed by the worked steps.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
You want one math program from counting through precalculus, beside any plan for other subjects.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Easy Peasy All-in-One Homeschool?
questions.answer: Easy Peasy places a learner with a test at the start, then follows a fixed order of daily lessons that the parent moves forward or back [3][5]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Easy Peasy All-in-One Homeschool work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of it on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [11][12].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. A family can keep Easy Peasy for other subjects and use AMP for math. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whichever course they were in.
